This project aims to leverage on this principle of combining multiple composite manufacturing processes namely large-scale AM of discontinuous reinforced composite with compression overmolding on top of additively manufactured metallic inserts. The resulting novel manufacturing process enables rapid design and manufacturing of lightweight automotive seats. The project seeks to develop a novel manufacturing process through which polymer composite preforms with controlled fiber orientation can be overmolded on to metal inserts at a rapid processing cycle time producing low porosity parts for the automotive seats. The novel manufacturing technique would also be relevant to a broad range of structural applications across all vehicles sub-systems. The development of a novel manufacturing process to achieve weight reduction in a car seat back is carried out through the tasks outlined below: • Design optimization of lightweight seatback frame through numerical modeling, topology optimization in commercially available finite element (FE) software, ABAQUS. • Development and testing of a novel additive manufacturing – compression molding (AM-CM) technique. • Design optimization of subcomponent with polymer composite overmolding on a metallic lattice structure. • Fabrication, experimental testing, and numerical modeling of the overmolding parts to investigate their mechanical performance. • Automation technology development for the AM polymer composite preform overmolding and exploration of smart sensor system integration, and • Final performance evaluation of the lightweight seatback enabled by the novel manufacturing process via numerical simulations. 2 | P age 3. MATERIALS AND MANUFACTURING PROCESS 3.1 Polymer Composite Preform Manufacturing In this study, carbon fiber-filled acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (20% wt. CF/ABS) SFT and carbon fiber reinforced polyamide-6,6 (40% wt. CF/PA66) LFT were used as the feedstock materials. An extrusion- based large scale additive manufacturing system known as BAAM, developed by Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) that use pelletized feedstock for rapid deposition (45 kg/hr) [2] was used to fabricate polymer composite preforms. The large-scale AM process is capable of rapidly manufacturing complex structures with little material waste [3,4]. BAAM produces composite structures with high anisotropy, where the fibers are highly aligned in the direction of the deposition [5]. The BAAM system is capable of printing both the SFT and LFT materials using pelletized feedstock materials. The mechanical properties of both the SFT and LFT solid panels are highly dependent on the fiber alignment resulted by the deposition pattern and melt flow properties of the polymer composite [6,7]. Here, BAAM was used to obtain 40% wt. CF/PA66 LFT preforms whereas robotic arm extruder was used to obtain 20% wt. CF/ABS SFT preforms. First, the 40% wt. CF/PA66 LFT pellets were used as feedstock material in this work (Techmer PM, TN, USA). Pellets were dried at 700 C for 8 h before use to remove moisture. A single-screw extruder mounted on the Cincinnati Inc. BAAM that is fitted with a 10.16 mm diameter nozzle was used to deposit 40% wt. CF/PA66 in a rectilinear pattern to obtain single- and double-layer composite preform, as shown in Fig. 3.1(a).
